summary: The Imperial calculator turns the length in inches, the area in square kilometers and more into temperature in degrees Fahrenheit. Think of it as a shortcut for a recipe, a shopping list, a travel plan or a form that asks for a unit you do not use. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Imperial calculator work?
sections.html:
The Imperial calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports temperature in degrees Fahrenheit in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the type of conversion); then you type in the length in inches, the area in square kilometers, the volume in teaspoons and the weight in grams.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 5 options, such as area, length and temperature. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in inches. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in square kilometers. The unit chip switches it to any of the 24 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in cubic meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 40 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in grams. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Imperial calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Temperature in degrees Fahrenheit=temperature in degrees Celsius
Temperature in degrees Celsius=temperature in Kelvin
Length in centimeters=length in millimeters
Length in meters=length in millimeters
Length in kilometers=length in millimeters
Area in square centimeters=area in square millimeters

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Temperature, opening in Fahrenheit
  • Temperature, opening in Rankine
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in kelvins
  • Temperature, opening in Delisle
  • Temperature, opening in Newton
  • Temperature, opening in Réaumur
  • Temperature, opening in Rømer

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Imperial calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Filling in a form that asks for imperial or metric values
  • Reading a recipe written in units you do not use
  • Checking a product listing against the measurements you work with
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length in inches, the area in square kilometers and the volume in teaspoons — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Imperial calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, derived from the length in inches, the area in square kilometers and the volume in teaspoons. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Imperial calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length in inches, the area in square kilometers, the volume in teaspoons and the weight in grams, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temperature in degrees Fahrenheit in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temperature in degrees Fahrenheit opens in Fahrenheit and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Imperial calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
